summary: Describes a SIP interface to VoiceXML media services. Application servers that control media servers commonly use it for pure VoiceXML processing, as an adjunct to the full MEDIACTRL protocol and packages.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone menus that talk and listen are described in VoiceXML. This note shows how a server can ask a media machine over SIP to run one of them.

subtitle: How an application server uses plain SIP calls to start, run and end VoiceXML dialogs on a media server.

tldr.problem: Telephony applications need a standard way to hand a caller to a media server that runs a VoiceXML voice dialog, and to get results back, without inventing a private control protocol.
tldr.mechanism: A SIP INVITE to a fixed 'dialog' user, with URI parameters such as voicexml, starts a VoiceXML session. SIP and SDP carry the media, session variables expose SIP data to the script, and results return over HTTP or in the body of the SIP BYE.
tldr.outcome: The interface also defines call transfer with REFER or INVITE, minimum codecs, DTMF and security requirements, and works as an adjunct to the full MEDIACTRL protocol.

facts.label: Mandatory audio codecs
facts.value: G.711 mu-law and A-law (payload types 0 and 8)

today: RFC 5552 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It remains the definition of this SIP interface to VoiceXML media services, and it is described as an adjunct to the full MEDIACTRL protocol.

sections.title: The Delegation Model and Its Use Cases
sections.content:
RFC 5552 describes a SIP interface to VoiceXML media services. An Application Server controls a VoiceXML Media Server, a VoiceXML interpreter with SIP and the media processing needed to run dialogs. The Application Server delegates the human-machine interaction to VoiceXML documents on the media server, but stays in the signaling path and can react to results or other network events. This is sometimes called the delegation model.

The memo lists several settings: IVR services built on application servers, a PSTN IVR service node reached through a gateway, the 3GPP IMS Media Resource Function (where this is the Mr interface), and interaction with CCXML. Devices that know nothing of this specification should still be able to invoke VoiceXML services on a compliant media server.

The VoiceXML application itself is usually fetched over HTTP, and may live on a different server from the SIP Application Server or be stored locally on the media server.
sections.plainLanguage: A boss program asks a helper machine to run a talking-and-listening menu for a caller. The boss stays on the line and hears how it went.

sections.title: Starting, Preparing and Ending a Session
sections.content:
The SIP Request-URI identifies the service. Its user part is fixed to dialog, matching RFC 4240. Parameters tell the server what to run: voicexml (the URI of the first document), maxage and maxstale (cache control for HTTP fetches), method (get or post, default get), postbody, ccxml and aai (JSON values). Parameter names are case-insensitive, special characters must be URL-escaped, and the server must unescape them only once. Parameters in later re-INVITEs are ignored, so the running application cannot be swapped.

On an INVITE, the media server sends 100 Trying and fetches the document. The 200 OK means the document was fetched and parsed, and execution starts when the ACK arrives. Errors are specific: a malformed or repeated parameter, or a missing voicexml with no default page, gets 400 Bad Request; a document that cannot be fetched or parsed gets 500.

To prepare a session, the Application Server opens a media-less dialog (SDP with no media lines, or an answer with media ports set to 0). The application runs only after a later re-INVITE establishes media. This is useful for outbound calls, where RFC 3725 flow IV is recommended.

Either side can end the session with a BYE. On receiving one, the media server MUST reply 200 OK and throw the connection.disconnect.hangup event.
sections.plainLanguage: The call is addressed to a special name with notes attached saying which menu to run. The helper fetches the menu, says it is ready, and starts when the caller is connected. Either side can hang up.

sections.title: Session Variable Mappings
sections.content:
Information from the SIP INVITE is exposed to the VoiceXML script as session variables. For example, session.connection.local.uri is the To URI and session.connection.remote.uri is the From URI. The protocol name is sip and the version is 2.0.

The array session.connection.protocol.sip.headers holds the INVITE headers, keyed by lowercase non-compact name, and implementations MUST at least include call-id. The array session.connection.protocol.sip.requesturi holds the Request-URI parameters, with the ccxml and aai values parsed as JSON. The shortcuts session.connection.aai and session.connection.ccxml read these. The History-Info header fills session.connection.redirect, and session.connection.protocol.sip.media describes each active media stream and is updated after a re-INVITE.

Because names like call-id are not valid ECMAScript identifiers, they must be read with array notation.
sections.plainLanguage: Facts about the phone call, such as who called and which headers were used, are handed to the menu script as ready-made variables.

sections.title: Media, DTMF and Returning Data
sections.content:
The media server MUST support offer/answer (RFC 3264) and, if no offer arrives in the INVITE, makes one in its 200 OK. It MAY support early media (RFC 3960), and MUST allow media changes by re-INVITE, with UPDATE as a SHOULD. For audio it MUST support G.711 mu-law and A-law (RTP payload types 0 and 8). Video is optional; if offered, H.263 Baseline MUST be supported. DTMF events per RFC 4733 MUST be supported.

Data can come back to the Application Server in two ways. Over HTTP, standard VoiceXML elements such as submit or data post results, and the SIP Call-ID can correlate them with the session. Over SIP, the expr or namelist of an exit element, or the namelist of disconnect, is encoded in the body of the BYE sent by the media server as application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=utf-8. The reserved name __reason says whether the end came from disconnect or exit, and __exit carries a bare expr value.

The media server MAY also place such data in the 200 OK to a received BYE, which means delaying that reply, subject to the caller's timer F (default 32 seconds).
sections.plainLanguage: The helper can report what the caller said or pressed either by sending a web form or by tucking a short note into the goodbye message.

sections.title: Outbound Calls and Call Transfer
sections.content:
Outbound calls use third-party call control (RFC 3725), with flow IV recommended together with session preparation, so the callee is not kept waiting while the document is fetched.

VoiceXML can request a transfer, but using it in networks with Application Servers is NOT RECOMMENDED; the Application Server should route calls itself, based on returned data. If transfer is supported, the memo's mechanisms MUST be used. Three kinds exist:

  • Blind: the media server sends a REFER on the original dialog. After a 2xx reply it throws connection.disconnect.transfer and ends the session with a BYE.
  • Bridge: the media server invites the callee and mixes the two media streams, so it stays in the middle. It can end the callee leg on a hotword or when the maximum duration is reached.
  • Consultation: like bridge at first, but the streams are not mixed, and a REFER with a Replaces header then connects caller and callee. The media server learns success from a NOTIFY carrying a 200 OK sipfrag.

SIP failure responses map to VoiceXML results, for instance 404 maps to error.connection.baddestination.
sections.plainLanguage: If the menu needs to pass the caller to someone else, it can hand them over and leave, stay on the line mixing everyone, or first check that the other person answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A well-known address for a media service may invite exploitation, for example an invoked service may trigger a billing event. The media server is RECOMMENDED to authenticate requesting endpoints with standard SIP mechanisms and to authorize them by local policy.

For confidentiality, the media server MUST implement the sips: and https: schemes and S/MIME encoding of message bodies. It MUST support Secure RTP (SRTP) for confidentiality, authentication and replay protection of media, including RTCP. To limit denial of service, it is RECOMMENDED to offer local policies such as time limits on VoiceXML application execution.
sections.plainLanguage: Because anyone might try to use the helper, it should check who is asking, scramble private data, and stop menus that run too long.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered six parameters in the SIP/SIPS URI Parameters registry, following the Specification Required policy of RFC 3969: maxage, maxstale, method (predefined values get and post), postbody, ccxml and aai. The voicexml parameter is defined in the Request-URI section but is not in this list.
sections.plainLanguage: The new call-address notes were added to the official list so nobody else uses the same names for something different.
